result:
The town’s clockmaker retired on a Tuesday, leaving every clock in his shop set to a different time.

People assumed this was a final joke. He had always been precise in his work and unreliable in his humor.

His daughter came home to clear the shop. She found brass gears in teacups, invoices tucked into detective novels, and a drawer labeled IMPORTANT containing nothing but keys.

For three days she wound the clocks, hoping their ticking would make the sorting less lonely.

On the fourth, a woman arrived carrying a kitchen clock shaped like a lemon.

“Your father was fixing this.”

His daughter examined the tag. There was no price, only a date from eleven years earlier.

“I’m sorry,” she said. “I don’t know why he kept it so long.”

“Oh, it works.” The woman turned it over and inserted a battery. The second hand began its brisk circuit. “I brought it back whenever I needed an excuse to visit.”

They stood among the clocks.

“Would you like some tea?” his daughter asked.

The woman would.

Over the next month, other customers came: a widower with a watch that ran perfectly, a bus driver whose alarm needed no adjustment, a boy who had been told that clock repair required biscuits.

His daughter learned to replace batteries. Then straps. She found a handbook beneath the counter and began reading it during quiet afternoons.

She never did discover what the keys opened.

She put them in a better box, though, and kept the label.
